Press Release:


Driven Hunt II
By Thursday morning a band of 13 European hunters had killed 49 animals in a ongoing Driven Hunt in Limpopo province. Animal activists this week descended on the farms where the animals were killed, vehemently protesting the controversial practice. Local and international outrage has followed last Sunday’s Carte Blanche exposé of the hunt, which sees game herded down a dedicated path toward hunters waiting on raised scaffolds. Carte Blanche remains in hot pursuit.


Script:


DRIVEN HUNT 2

V/O: Last week Carte Blanche exposed the full scale of a planned driven hunt in Limpopo - 600 high seats erected on 3 farms spanning 9000 hectares north of Alldays. We asked for confirmation from the landowners, the Tshivhula Communal Property Association, but initially spokesperson Simon Mafela denied it.

Simon: There is nothing like a planned driven hunt.

V/O: But finally the main organizer and investor Anton de Vries gave us the facts: 13 hunters from Holland and Belgium would participate in a driven hunt over 5 days, if Limpopo Nature Conservation gave the go-ahead.

Marius: “Siren”

V/O: Our expose unleashed howls of condemnation from around the world. Petitions to stop the slaughter were signed by thousands. and the issue trended on every social media platform.

Marius: Kom uit daar julle sissies! Kom uit! Kom uit, kom wys julle gesigte!”

Subtitles: “Come out of there you sissies! Come out! Come out, come and show your faces!”

V/O; Anticipating a massacre, animal activists mobilized and descended on the farm to protest at the gates on Monday morning. The international media picked up the scent and soon the story went global.

Devi: September is tourism month in South Africa and this year Limpopo is the host province, but the debacle over driven hunting has overshadowed their good news stories.

V/O; The driven hunt went ahead, closely monitored by the Department of Environmental Affairs and inspectors from the NSPCA.

Isabel: They didn’t break any laws according to what they are permitted to do. If it’s something that’s going to stay legal, that’s the question.

V/O: Senior Inspector Isabel Wentzel explained how the driven hunt works on a rectangular grid.

Isabel: Animals are being pushed by a line of beaters in orange overalls. They are all numbered so that they stay in line. The guys walk, they talk quite a bit.


V/O The hunters are positioned on 3 sides of the rectangle, the beaters walk forward from the 4th side.

Isabel: The hunters face forward; the animals come from the back and they would shoot them on the road where the chairs are actually standing on.

V/O: Driven hunting is a European tradition and virtually unheard of in South Africa. We asked the South African Hunters and Game Conservation Association for comment.

Fred: If driven hunting is done in a legal way in the appropriate circumstances and in a responsible way, we would have no objection against driven hunting.

V/O: But CEO Fred Camphor feels the Limpopo valley is the wrong place for it.

Fred: Most of the vegitation is your Mopane bushveldt which is ideally suited for walk-and-stalk hunting. Using driven hunting in an area such as that we believe is inappropriate.

V/O: But the protestors believe it’s inhumane.

Devi: So you guys are with Wildlife Crimes…?

Natasha: …and other Murders.

Devi: And you drove from Durban?

Natasha: Yes.

Devi Silly question but why are you here?

Natasha: Well we don’t believe it’s ethical, and we want to show our support to the rest of South Africa and the other people that don’t approve of it.

Paul: Cruelty to an animal is not about the animal that gets shot, it’s about what exactly transpires to an animal until it gets shot.

V/O: Paul Oxton is the founder of Wild Heart Wildlife Foundation. Camped out at the gate he photographed all the foreign hunters.

Paul: A very big Belgian paper picked up on the story and went ahead and used the pictures from it.

Devi: Do you think some of the hunters were recognized by your picture and they feel embarrassed?

Paul: I believe they were.

V/O; At first the hunters seemed amused by all the attention, but after the second day they were hiding their faces. What was meant to be a luxury safari had turned into the hunter becoming the hunted.

Isabel: Their faces were published overseas, some people have actually received death threats.

Devi: But from whom?

Isabel: From people in their own towns.

V/O: So when the NSPCA tried to bring in their own cameraman to film the hunt, the organizers refused.

Isabel: So the situation got a bit tense there, and in the end we were actually thrown off the farm.

V/O: Undeterred they drove back into Alldays for help.

Devi: The NSPCA in order to enforce the warrant had to get the local police, and they’ve just arrived.

V/O: The police ensured that the NSPCA would be able to film on Braam farm the next day. But when they arrived there was no hunt. Instead they were able to inspect the area where the animal skins were being treated, and the skulls cleaned. In the cold room only a few carcasses remained, including that of a duiker. It was evident that this area had been stacked with dead animals, but had been cleared out the night before.

V/O: Anton de Vries told us that many of the animals on the farm were recently bought at auction.

Fred: In the view of the association, that’s completely inappropriate. We do not support put and take operations at all.

Sfx: Beep, beep.

Marius: Hulle is lus vir jou op Weipe de Vries! Kom saam met my, ek sal jou vat. Jy kan saam met my ry. Laat die jou boere goed bliksem!
They want to fight you at Weipe de Vries. Come with me, I’ll take you. You can ride with me. Let the farmers give you a good hiding!

V/O: On Thursday another posse of protestors arrived from Louis Trichardt, Johannesburg and Pretoria. Every car that went in or out of the gate was given the same treatment.. We also met a former owner of Ammondale, Pieter Exley.

Devi: How did you feel when you saw the story on Sunday?

Pieter: I sat crying, I couldn’t believe what I was seeing. I couldn’t believe people were going to such an awful standard of hunting.

V/O: Rosarie Kemp is a veterinary nurse and breeds buffalo.

Roasarie: I’m here to support hunters, and I know it sounds strange but hunting is part of what we do in this area. I just want to show that whatever that guy is doing is not hunting, and he makes us that do hunting the right way and with the right permits look really bad in the whole world.

Marius: I don’t agree with this type of hunting. To me it’s not hunting, it’s a massacre. If the sport cannot be – you can’t even call it a sport – here they are.

V/O: Inexplicably the organisers decided to hold a drive right next to the road where they could be easily spotted.

Devi: These are the beaters that we’ve been talking about. They all have numbers on the back of their uniforms, all dressed in orange. But now they’re on a completely different farm. This is Ammondale, far away from Braam where the SPCA has been visiting with their cameraman.

Camera: How much are you guys getting paid today?

Beater: 120 a day.

Camera: 120?

Beater: Per day.

V/O: After a few minutes the hunt began, with the protestors looking on helplessly, knowing what was to come.

Devi: The beaters have just left, walked into the bush. I wouldn’t be surprised if pretty soon we are going to hear gunshots.

V/O: Way off in the distance we could see the hunters on the platforms, but the animals had no idea they were there.

Sfx: Beaters shouting and gunshots.

V/O: On the platforms the hunters waited silently for the animals to appear, rifles at the ready.

Hunter: They don’t want to come to this camp, maybe because of the wind. They smell us.

Sfx: The shot missed its target.

Devi: What did it feel like for you watching those animals being killed, but you had a job to do, you had to monitor the situation?

Isabel: It’s not a nice feeling. Just…I don’t like what I see. I don’t enjoy what I see.

Devi: The driven hunt went ahead this week despite the international outcry. So we came to Alldays to follow it, only to discover that driven hunting has been going on here for years.

V/O: Just north of the Soutpansberg is Goro Game Reserve. Several viewers claimed driven hunts have been held here since 2001.
Flying over the farm we could just make out the hunting platforms dotted around the grid laid out for the hunts.

Dave Dewsnap is the farm manager.

Devi: Do you do driven hunting on your farm at Goro?

Dave: I do.

Devi: So you see no problem with driven hunting?

Dave: No, I see it as a sustained utilization of a natural resource

Devi: Explain that?

Dave: This land specifically is marginal land. It’s not good enough for crops and irrigation, it’s not really good enough for cattle. And the wild animals are the only ones who really know how to use it.

Devi: How long have you been involved in driven hunting on this farm?

Dave: About 14 years.

Devi: So it goes back as long as that?

Dave: It goes back as long as that.

V/O: Fourteen years ago “Johanna” was an assistant manager at Goro.

Devi: Who owned the farm at the time?

Johanna: Mark Diks

Devi: Who is Mark Diks?

Dave: Mark Diks or was a business man from Belgium.

V/O; Mark Diks - seen here in the green baseball cap - is one of the wealthiest men in Europe. A keen hunter he also invited friends and family to these driven hunts.

Johanna: After a day’s hunt that went well, they will pile up all the animals to... to see how much they have killed in one day. Of all the animals that has been shot at least two thirds would have been wounded.

Devi: So who goes and finds those wounded animals and puts them out of their misery?

Johanna: We would, after hours.

Dave: There’s no more wounding in a driven hunt – pro rata by number of guns, by number of animals shot – than there are per individuals hunting walk and stalk.

Devi: So there were animals that were wounded?

Isabel: Yes, not the majority, But there were a couple of them that they had to go and track.

V/O According to the NSPCA the final tally for this week is 98 animals killed. But decisions around the future of driven hunting no longer lie with Limpopo.

Isabel: Yes, it has escalated from provincial to Environmental Affairs, because they are now looking into it. So it’s become a national issue.














DRIVEN HUNT 2 PROMOS

Promo 1 (15”):

Link: The driven hunt went ahead this week despite the international outcry. So we came to Alldays to follow it, only to discover that driven hunting has been going on here for years.

V/O: New pictures have emerged of controversial driven hunts in Limpopo.

Promo 2 (15”)

Marius: The one beater I saw, but behind him was a big truck full of these peop0le with orange overalls on, obviously to chase the animals to the hunters.

V/O: We go back to Alldays and bring you footage of the controversial driven hunt.


Promo 3 (10”)

Devi: The beaters have just left, walked into the bush. I wouldn’t be surprised if pretty soon we are going to hear gunshots.

V/O: We witness the driven hunt in Alldays.
